title: Kernel priming & warmup experiments — flash/paged/fused ops
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a compact record of small-batch experiments aimed at reducing first-request and tail latency caused by kernel/JIT/cold-cache effects for attention kernels (FlashAttention variants, paged attention, and fused operator chains). These notes are intentionally pragmatic — quick commands, numbers, and hypotheses we can act on before a larger benchmark sweep.

Background / motivation:
- We see sporadic p95/p99 blips on newly provisioned or autoscaled nodes. Root cause candidates: kernel launch overhead (JIT/compilation or kernel selection), page faults / GPU memory allocation hot paths, and cold KV-cache memory misses for long-context requests.
- Customer-facing SLO: 99th percentile generation latency under 350ms for interactive workloads (seq<=128, batch=1). Some environments currently miss this during node spin-up or after model swap.

Test environment (short):
- Runtime: rwd-rt-1.7.2 (internal nightly build with improved scheduler hooks)
- Hardware: H100-80GB (dev cluster h100-pool-2), CUDA 12.2, Ubuntu 22.04
- Models: open-13B (dense), quantized 8-bit variant (q8_stable) -- model name used: open-13B-q8
- Kernel variants evaluated: FlashAttention2 fused (FA2-fused), PagedFlash (paged with 64KB pages), FusedLinear+Attn (operator fusion prototype).
- Workloads: short interactive (seq_in=32, gen=32, batch=1), medium chat (seq=128, batch=1), long-context (seq=512, batch=1 and batch=4).
- Measurement: p50/p95/p99 latency for total generation and kernel hotpath times (where trace available). Each experiment ran 200 steady-state requests after warmup, and we recorded the very-first request separately.

Experiment A: synthetic-prefix priming (KV cache seeding)
- Method: For models with KV cache (decoder-only), before serving real requests we issue a synthetic "seed" token sequence of length 64 with batch size matching expected traffic. This forces KV allocation and warms attention cache paths.
- Command (simplified): ./run_warmup.sh --model open-13B-q8 --priming-tokens 64 --batch 1 --variant FA2-fused
- Observations:
  - First-request latency (no priming): 1st = 1120ms, steady p99 = 420ms
  - With 64-token priming: 1st = 220ms, steady p99 = 370ms (~12% p99 improvement), steady p50 unchanged
  - For seq=512 workload: first-request improvement bigger (1st down 1700ms -> 310ms), steady p99 down ~28%
- Notes: priming helps dramatically for the first request and reduces p99 for long-context cases. Overhead of running the priming itself is ~50-80ms per node and can be amortized across expected requests.

Experiment B: micro-batch kernel priming (JIT / kernel selection)
- Method: Launch small synthetic batches (batch=4, seq=64) to force kernel selection and possible JIT paths. Compare to no-op warmup that just touches memory (cudaMalloc/free loop).
- Observations:
  - JIT-priming (run small-generation) reduces 1st request latency by ~550ms for FA2-fused. The cudaMalloc-touch only reduced ~120ms.
  - For FA2-fused the priming run produced a measurable decrease in kernel launch variance (p99 kernel time down ~18%).
  - For PagedFlash the benefit is smaller; paged attention already has longer steady kernel times but less startup jitter.
- Hypothesis: some of our kernel-selection code paths trigger slower kernels on cold runs (e.g., code that probes different tiling strategies). Running a small workload caches the heuristic decisions.

Experiment C: fused-op chain warmup vs memory fragmentation
- Method: prime fused linear+attn chains by running a few requests that exercise the full fused path. Also measure GPU memory fragment size via cuda-meminfo snapshots before/after.
- Observations:
  - Fused chains deliver lower steady-state latency for batch sizes >=4, but the initial warmup increases max resident memory slightly due to temporary buffers allocated by the fused kernel (~+1.2GB measured).
  - In one run repeated warmups across multiple consecutive model swaps caused fragmentation-like behavior and later kernel allocations hit slower allocation paths (p99 increases).
- Recommendation: run a compact allocation hammer after fuse warmup to consolidate memory pools (we used cuMemPoolTrim equivalent). Avoid running huge numbers of fuse-warmup requests back-to-back without pool trimming.

Experiment D: paged-attention specific observation (page prefetch distance)
- Method: test different page prefetch distances (how aggressively we prefetch next KV pages: distances tested 0, 1, 4 pages ahead) under mixed seq-length workloads.
- Observations:
  - Prefetch distance = 1 reduced tail latency for mixed traffic with a modest memory cost. p99 for seq512 mixed dropped ~9%.
  - Prefetch distance = 4 gave diminishing returns and increased memory churn; also sometimes increased p50 for small requests due to background IO.
- Conclusion: conservative prefetch (1 page) is a good default; dynamic heuristic that increases prefetch for sustained long-context sessions looks promising.

Lightweight numeric summary (representative):
- short (seq<=64, batch=1): 1st w/o priming 420ms -> with priming 180ms; steady p99 310ms -> 295ms
- med (seq=128, batch=1): 1st 740ms -> 210ms; steady p99 380ms -> 345ms
- long (seq=512, batch=1): 1st 1700ms -> 310ms; steady p99 540ms -> 390ms
Numbers are noisy; run-to-run variance +/- 4-9% depending on background host load.

Operational tradeoffs / cost:
- Warmup work consumes GPU cycles and costs money for hosted nodes. However, the priming run is tiny (tens of ms for a few requests) compared to the customer-visible first-request penalty (hundreds to thousands ms).
- For Dedicated nodes with reserved capacity, automatic warmup on model load is an obvious win. For ephemeral autoscaling hosts, consider targeted warmup only for nodes predicted to receive low-latency traffic (use router hints).

Recommendations / next actions:
1) Implement a lightweight per-model "priming_profile" that specifies: priming token length, priming batch size, and kernel-priming enabled flag. Default for decoder-only models: tokens=64, batch=1, kernel_priming=true.
2) Add a node-start hook in dedicated/hosted agents: run priming_profile on model activation and publish "primed:true" tag to the router. Router can prefer primed nodes for latency-sensitive traffic for first N minutes.
3) For fused-ops, integrate a memory-pool-trim after warmup to prevent fragmentation accumulation. We need a small patch to runtime to expose trimming API.
4) Run a 48-hour mixed-workload soak with and without priming enabled to measure long-tail effects (Jira: JIRA-RT-789, linked).
5) Create a small perf doc for SRE/ops describing the costs and toggles (how to disable priming for cost-sensitive tenants).

Open questions / TODO:
- Does priming interact badly with model-quantization caches (q8 vs q4)? Quick check showed similar benefits but we need a systematic sweep.
- Should priming be adaptive (only run if node predicts immediate traffic)? Need router telemetry to decide.
- Investigate kernel-selection heuristics that still probe multiple kernels on the first request; maybe persist kernel choices to a small node-level cache keyed by (model, seq, batch) to avoid future probes.

Notes to self / messy log:
- run 2024-11-12: used trace-20241112-priming-run; saw unexpected p50 inflation for tiny requests when priming ran concurrently — likely prefetch background work interfering with small-tail allocations.
- Diego: follow up on cuMemPoolTrim integration (PR in platform repo).
- Sofia: can you add a flag in model config UI for "prefer-primed-nodes"?

Attachments / quick links:
- trace-20241112-priming-run (linked_artifacts)
- JIRA-RT-789 (evaluation soak ticket)

Bottom line: simple, cheap priming (64 tokens + small kernel exercise) reliably fixes most first-request pain and reduces p99 for long-context workloads. We should gate rollouts behind a soak test and add careful memory trimming for fused ops to avoid long-term fragmentation.
